title: How contingency leaves lasting paths
summary: Wars, disasters and personal choices cannot always be deduced from long-term structures. An event may redirect a society toward a path it has not previously taken. Recognizing structural conditions does not eliminate contingency.

blocks.text: Wars, disasters and personal choices cannot always be deduced from long-term structures. An event may redirect a society toward a path it has not previously taken. Recognizing structural conditions does not eliminate contingency.

Yet contingency does not act on an empty field. The same shock can have different consequences within different institutions, resources and networks. Whether a decision leaves a lasting mark depends on how it is subsequently organized, reproduced and maintained.

Established routes, rules and knowledge shape later choices. Resources have already been invested, and people have learned to cooperate in familiar ways. Changing direction therefore carries costs. Path dependence explains this accumulation without implying that the past has closed the future.

Understanding divergence requires attention to both events and accumulated conditions. An unexpected change can open a direction that existing capabilities support or constrain. History is neither an inevitable program nor a sequence of unrelated accidents.
